title: The Old Babylonian 'Pennsylvania tablet'
short: Most of Thompson's Tablet II comes from an Old Babylonian tablet (c. 1700 BC) in Philadelphia, older and different in wording from the Nineveh version.
body: Thompson's note marks this column 'Old Babylonian Version'. The tablet, published by Langdon (1917) and re-edited by Jastrow and Clay (1920), covers the meeting of the heroes, Enkidu's humanisation and their fight. Its language differs from the later standard version (e.g. 'Uruk of the broad squares' instead of 'Uruk-the-Sheepfold'). Thompson thus combines texts about a thousand years apart; modern editions (George 2003) print them as separate versions. Tigay used such tablets to show how the epic evolved: the Old Babylonian poem was not simply copied but revised and expanded in the later version attributed to Sin-leqi-unninni.

title: 'Nymph', 'doxy': Thompson's names for the courtesan
short: Thompson calls the courtesan 'the nymph' and Gilgamish later calls her 'doxy': archaic English for an unnamed woman whose Old Babylonian name is Shamkatum.
body: In the Old Babylonian text the woman is named Samkatum (the later Samhat); Thompson treats the word as a description and avoids naming her, choosing English words with literary colour: 'nymph' (a Greek nature-spirit, also a beautiful young woman) and 'doxy' (Elizabethan slang for a beggar's mistress or prostitute). The choice illustrates Thompson's general method of using archaic, classicising diction (hetaera, aegis, Hades, vaward) to give the poem epic dignity in hexameters. Students should remember that these are the translator's words, not the Babylonian ones.

title: 'Erech broad-marketed'
short: 'Broad-marketed' renders the Old Babylonian epithet 'Uruk of the broad squares' (rebitu, an open square or street).
body: The Old Babylonian poet's favourite epithet for the city stresses its public spaces, where people gather; Thompson's 'broad-marketed' interprets the squares as market-places. In the later standard version the usual epithet is instead 'Uruk-the-Sheepfold' (Thompson's 'the high-wall'd'). The broad street is also where the crowds gather to admire Enkidu, and where he blocks Gilgamish's path, so the epithet suits the public drama of this tablet.

title: The shepherds' camp: a stage of civilisation
short: The courtesan leads Enkidu first to the shepherds' camp: between wild steppe and city lies the pastoral world.
body: The sequence of Enkidu's progress is carefully graded: wild animals, then shepherds, then the city. The woman shares her clothing with him, and the shepherds offer him food. Scholars have read this as a Mesopotamian theory of civilisation, in which pastoralism is an intermediate stage. Enkidu then protects the shepherds from lions and wolves, becoming their watchman: a man who once freed animals from traps now hunts them. The reversal is echoed when Gilgamish, grieving, puts on skins and roams the steppe (VIII-X).

title: Bread and beer
short: Enkidu does not know how to eat bread or drink; the woman teaches him that bread is 'the essential of life' and drink the custom of the land.
body: Bread and beer were the staples of Mesopotamian diet and the basic rations paid to workers; they stand for cultivated, cooked food as opposed to the milk of wild animals that Enkidu had sucked. Thompson's 'mead' renders sikaru, which is beer (barley-beer), not honey-wine; Jastrow and Clay speak of 'food and strong drink'. Seven cups make Enkidu merry: a humorous scene that is also a rite of passage. Shamash later reminds Enkidu that the woman fed him bread 'fit for divinity' and drink 'fit for royalty' (VII).

title: 'And thus became human'
short: After food, drink, washing and anointing with oil, Enkidu 'became a man' (awilis iwe): humanity is defined by culture, not birth.
body: The verb means 'he turned into a man'. Grooming is the final stage: the body hair is rubbed with oil, and he puts on a garment. In Mesopotamia oil and clothing were basic tokens of civilised life (and oil and clothes were standard rations). The scene is mirrored in reverse when Gilgamish lets himself become unwashed and clad in skins while mourning, and then is washed and dressed in a clean garment at Uta-Napishtim's command (XI). Thompson's note suggests 'man' could also be 'bridegroom' in the next line, a reading that points ahead to the wedding scene.

title: Enkidu as watchman
short: Enkidu hunts the lions and wolves that attack the flocks, so that the shepherds sleep: the former friend of animals becomes their enemy.
body: Thompson's note on 'soundly' remarks on an unclear use of a word for 'greatness'. The point of the episode is reversal: the man who had once filled in the trapper's pits now guards the herds. Lions and wolves (Thompson 'jackals') are the predators that threaten civilised order; Gilgamish will kill lions at the mountain passes (IX), and Ea's speech in Tablet XI proposes lions and wolves as alternatives to the Flood.

title: The 'House of Community' (bit emuti)
short: Thompson's 'House of Community' renders bit emuti, which modern editors take as the 'house of the in-laws', i.e. a wedding-house.
body: Thompson explains the phrase as the common meeting place of the men of the town, comparing Arab villages of his day. Modern scholarship (George 2003) takes emutu to mean the relationship by marriage, so the stranger is going to a wedding feast, to which he brings the customary gifts. This makes better sense of what follows: the king is about to claim the bride before the bridegroom. The difference is a good example of how philology since 1928 has changed the meaning of the narrative.

title: The king's 'right of the first night'
short: Gilgamish sleeps with the 'wife of destiny' (the bride) before her husband: the clearest statement of the tyranny that Enkidu stops.
body: Thompson admits that he used a euphemism here and that the text is very difficult. Modern editors translate: 'He will couple with the wife-to-be, he first, the husband after.' The custom resembles the medieval ius primae noctis, though whether such a right was ever practised in Mesopotamia is unknown, and George treats it as a literary motif of tyranny. The stranger presents it as decreed by the gods 'from the moment his umbilical cord was cut'. Enkidu's outrage at hearing this motivates his blocking of the door.

title: Enkidu as Gilgamish's double
short: The crowd sees at once that Enkidu is Gilgamish's match: slightly shorter, but stronger in bone.
body: Aruru was told to make a 'counterpart' to Gilgamish (I); here the people confirm the likeness. The theme of the double or second self is central: Enkidu absorbs the king's excess energy, shares his adventures, and dies in a sense in his place. Scholars have compared other pairs of heroes (Achilles and Patroclus, David and Jonathan). The crowd's joy suggests that the city sees in Enkidu a deliverer from its oppressor.

title: The couch of Ishhara
short: 'The couch for the love-rites' is literally 'for Ishhara', a goddess of love and of oaths, associated with marriage.
body: Thompson's note: 'Lit. "for Ishhara," the goddess of love.' Ishhara was a goddess of Syrian origin, linked with Ishtar, invoked at marriages and in oaths. The bed is laid for her as for a wedding: the scene is a nuptial ceremony, and Gilgamish approaches as the king who takes the bride. Enkidu stands in the doorway; the fight at the threshold is a fight about marriage and kingship.

title: The fight at the door
short: The two heroes wrestle 'like bulls', shattering the doorpost and shaking the wall, until Gilgamish bends his knee and his anger subsides.
body: The wrestling match is the turning point of the first part of the poem: rivalry becomes friendship. The simile of fighting bulls recalls Gilgamish's image as a wild bull (I) and anticipates the killing of the Bull of Heaven (VI). Who wins is not quite clear: Gilgamish 'bent his leg to the ground', which may mean he pinned Enkidu or that he himself knelt. Many critics think the ambiguity is deliberate, since the fight ends without a defeated party and with Enkidu praising Gilgamish's kingship. Thompson's note suggests 'ardour' could also be 'rage' (literally 'breast').

title: 'Cow of the steer-folds'
short: Enkidu praises Gilgamish as the unique son of Nin-sun, 'the wild cow of the fold': Thompson's 'cow of the steer-folds'.
body: Nin-sun's name already means 'Lady Wild Cow', and her standard epithet calls her the wild cow of the fold; her son is the 'wild bull'. The fold (supuru) is the same word as in the city epithet 'Uruk-the-Sheepfold'. By praising his mother and the kingship bestowed by Enlil, Enkidu acknowledges Gilgamish's legitimacy; the speech turns the fight into an alliance.

title: Nin-sun, mother of Gilgamish
short: Nin-sun ('Lady Wild Cow') is the goddess-mother of Gilgamish, wife of Lugal-banda.
body: Thompson's note: 'The mother of Gilgamish.' Her Sumerian name means 'Lady Wild Cow'. A minor goddess, she was worshipped in the region of Uruk and in the epic lives in the 'Palace of Splendour' (Egalmah). Her divinity explains the hero's 'two-thirds' divine nature. In Tablet III she prays for her son and, in George's text, adopts Enkidu. Her wisdom as an interpreter of dreams has already been shown in Tablet I.

title: Kingship bestowed by Enlil
short: Enlil, the executive of the gods, grants kingship: Enkidu ends the fight by recognising Gilgamish's divine right to rule.
body: In the Sumerian King List 'kingship descended from heaven', and Enlil was the god who conferred it. Enkidu's words are a formal acknowledgement that the king, whatever his excesses, is legitimate. The friendship now replaces the tyranny: the epic does not depose the bad king but redirects his energy toward an expedition that will bring fame. Gilgamish's ancestry in the King List (after Lugal-banda) is noted in Thompson's preface.
